entries.issuing_body: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
entries.title: Eighth Circuit affirms vacatur of the Federal Reserve's 21-cent debit interchange fee cap and remands Regulation II to the Board
entries.facts: In No. 25-3000, filed October 26, 2026, a unanimous Eighth Circuit panel (Judges L.R. Smith, Benton and Stras, with Judge Stras writing) held that the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System exceeded its authority under the Durbin Amendment by setting debit interchange fees on costs that are not specific to an individual transaction. The court affirmed the district court judgment vacating the current 21-cent cap and remanded for the agency to come up with a fee structure that reflects the statute Congress wrote, stating that the Board must at a minimum sort costs into transaction-specific and non-transaction-specific categories. The opinion states that its decision becomes effective only when the mandate issues, which its footnote 5 describes as seven days after the deadline to petition for rehearing or after an order denying rehearing, and that parties have 45 days to seek rehearing in cases involving a federal agency. Until the mandate issues, the existing cap remains in effect. The court did not set a new cap and did not reach the remaining challenges.
entries.source_label: Opinion, No. 25-3000 (8th Cir., filed October 26, 2026), U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit opinions directory
entries.relevant_to: card issuers, acquirers, payment processors, merchants and payment-facilitation platforms

entries.title: FinCEN issues alert FIN-2026-Alert009 on foreign-agent-directed transactions through U.S. money services businesses, citing more than 8 billion dollars in suspicious payments
entries.facts: On October 30, 2026 FinCEN issued FIN-2026-Alert009, titled FinCEN Alert on Risks Associated with Foreign-Agent-Directed Transactions. FinCEN states it identified more than 8 billion dollars in suspicious foreign-agent-directed payments between 2021 and 2025. The alert describes a typology in which foreign agents direct a U.S. principal money services business to pay third-party entities abroad under cross-border settlement arrangements, obscuring ultimate beneficiaries and the purpose of the transactions. It sets out red-flag indicators for principal money services businesses and separately for banks serving them, including payments to third parties not covered by the agent clearing agreement, recurring payments to recipients in China, the United Arab Emirates, Egypt and East African countries including Kenya, Uganda and Djibouti, vague stated purposes such as settlement, services or business expense, round or near-round dollar amounts, and agent reluctance to document recipients or disclose licensing and AML/CFT controls. FinCEN instructs institutions to reference the key term FIN2026FOREIGNAGENT in SAR field 2 and in the narrative, and for Form 8300 filings to include the term in the Comments section and select Box 1b.
entries.relevant_to: money services businesses, money transmitters, banks serving MSBs, cross-border payment providers

entries.title: FTC and eight state enforcers sue a restaurant point-of-sale and payment-processing provider over undisclosed fees, unauthorized add-ons and cancellation practices
entries.facts: On October 29, 2026 the FTC announced that it, the People of California through the Los Angeles County Counsel and the San Francisco City Attorney, and the Attorneys General of Colorado, Florida, Illinois, Iowa, Nebraska, Oklahoma and Utah filed suit in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California against a restaurant point-of-sale, software and payment-processing provider and affiliated entities, on a 2 to 0 Commission vote, alleging violations of the FTC Act and the Restore Online Shoppers Confidence Act. The complaint alleges that merchants were enrolled in and charged for add-on services without consent; that Pay-as-you-Go plan terms were not clearly disclosed, including a requirement to return hardware or pay its full retail value if payment processing did not begin within 120 days, an 85 dollar monthly payment-processing charge during temporary closures, and a 150 dollar per remaining month early termination fee; that from September 2021 to late July 2023 a 99 cent fee was added to certain online orders over 10 dollars and retained by the defendant rather than the restaurant; that cancellation required an undisclosed 30-day written notice and was met with unanswered notices and retention offers, with one merchant charged a 5,318.87 dollar early termination fee; that cancelling a subscription or switching providers was treated as default on the defendant's merchant loans, triggering immediate repayment of the outstanding balance; and that 24/7/365 support claims were false. The FTC release states no settlement, monetary amount, order terms or deadlines, and says the court will decide the case.
entries.relevant_to: point-of-sale and merchant-services providers, payment processors, subscription billing and embedded-lending platforms

entries.title: SEC charges two entities over a 130 million dollar crypto wealth-sharing scheme that allegedly used false Form ADV and Form D filings as proof of registration
entries.facts: In press release 2026-110, dated October 29, 2026, the SEC announced a complaint filed in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California against two foreign-operated, Colorado-incorporated entities. The SEC alleges that from at least October 2025 through June 2026 they raised more than 130 million dollars from tens of thousands of retail investors in more than 40 states and several U.S. territories through a wealth-sharing program promising risk-free returns from crypto asset trading signals; that one entity falsely claimed to be the world's largest hedge fund and an SEC-registered investment adviser partnered with the other as a licensed and secure crypto trading platform; that both filed false Form ADV and Form D documents with the SEC which investors could view and treated as proof of SEC licensing or approval; that fake certificates bearing the SEC seal were displayed; and that periodic Ponzi-like payments were made to some investors while remaining funds were misappropriated, with solicitation through social media, encrypted messaging, weekly live videoconferences and a mobile app. The SEC charged antifraud provisions of the Securities Act of 1933 and the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 against both entities and Sections 204(a) and 207 of the Investment Advisers Act of 1940 against one, seeking permanent injunctions, disgorgement with prejudgment interest, civil penalties and conduct-based injunctions. The SEC states it removed the two filings from its website and that the Alberta Securities Commission and state agencies in Hawaii, Texas, Utah, Washington and Wisconsin assisted.
entries.relevant_to: crypto trading platforms, investment advisers, retail-facing digital-asset marketers

entries.title: SR-NYSEAMER-2026-96 modifies NYSE American binary return derivatives rules, effective on filing with the 30-day operative delay waived and comments due November 30, 2026
entries.facts: At 91 FR 68563, published October 30, 2026 as Federal Register document 2026-22132, the SEC published notice of filing and immediate effectiveness of SR-NYSEAMER-2026-96 (Release 34-106743, notice dated October 27, 2026), a proposed rule change filed by NYSE American LLC on October 21, 2026 modifying its Binary Return Derivatives, or ByRDs, rules. The filing sets the settlement price as the underlying security's closing price on the primary listing market instead of a full-day composite volume-weighted average price; eliminates the rule rounding the settlement price up one cent when it equals a strike price, so that Finish High ByRDs pay 100 dollars if the underlying closes at or above the strike and Finish Low ByRDs pay 100 dollars if it closes below; deletes Rule 900ByRDs(b)(4) and renumbers the following paragraphs; specifies a fixed 100 dollar cash settlement amount; raises the minimum individual-stock market capitalization for listing from 40 billion dollars to 290 billion dollars and adds a requirement of at least 10 million dollars average daily trading value in the primary market's closing auction over the prior six months for both initial and continued listing, which the exchange says would reduce eligible underliers from 305 to approximately 100; removes the requirement that Market Makers continuously quote in automatically appointed ByRDs classes; and excludes ByRDs from the Price Reasonability Checks in Rule 928.1NYP while adding a class-level maximum price protection that rejects limit orders and quotes above it. The filing was made under Rule 19b-4(f)(6) and has become effective pursuant to Section 19(b)(3)(A). The Commission waived the 30-day operative delay and designated the proposal operative upon filing. Comments are due on or before November 30, 2026.
entries.relevant_to: binary-options and event-contract venues, options market makers, prediction-market platforms

entries.title: FinCEN issues notice FIN-2026-NTC2 on the use of charities and non-profit organizations for illicit activity
entries.facts: On October 30, 2026 FinCEN issued FIN-2026-NTC2, titled FinCEN Notice on the Use of Charities and Non-Profit Organizations for Illicit Activity. The notice describes three schemes: sham charity schemes, in which an entity advertises a legitimate purpose while using the non-profit for illicit activity including funnelling money to terrorist organizations; non-profit fraud schemes, in which operators enrich themselves while providing few or no services and divert donations or government funds; and non-profit embezzlement schemes, in which insiders or contractors steal from an otherwise legitimately operating organization. Red flags are grouped by the organization and its officers or employees, by sources of funds and by uses of funds, and include solicitation with little or no services or physical presence, names resembling well-known organizations, absent state registration or verifiable legal status, officers with prior fraud convictions, sudden surges of donations or government reimbursements at recently formed organizations, payments intended for the organization landing in personal accounts, minimal operating costs apart from social media advertising or vague consulting fees, patterns suggesting evasion of reporting requirements or structuring of cash, and significant transfers abroad by U.S.-focused organizations. FinCEN instructs institutions to reference the key term FIN2026NPO in SAR field 2 and in the narrative.
entries.relevant_to: banks, money services businesses and payment processors with non-profit customers
